subject: human stomach
title: A Man Lived 58 Years With a Hole Into His Stomach. His Doctor Used It

scenes.text: In 1822 a shotgun blew open a man's side. The hole never closed.
Alexis St. Martin was shot from a meter away on Mackinac Island. His surgeon, William Beaumont, expected him to die.
He didn't. His stomach wall healed onto his skin, leaving a permanent opening under his ribs with a flap you could push in.
So Beaumont tied beef, bread and cabbage to silk strings, lowered them into the stomach, and pulled them out hours later.
Over 200 experiments proved digestion is chemical: an acid dissolves food. Vials of stomach juice rode in St. Martin's armpits to stay warm.
He lived to 1880, 27 years longer than his doctor. His family let his body rot and buried it eight feet deep, so no one could take the stomach.

description:
A hunting-store accident in 1822 gave medicine its first window into a living human stomach.
On 6 June 1822 Alexis St. Martin was shot at close range on Mackinac Island. He survived, but the wound healed with the stomach wall fused to the skin, leaving a permanent fistula. Army surgeon William Beaumont ran around 200 experiments between 1825 and 1833, lowering food tied to silk strings into the stomach, timing digestion and collecting gastric juice, and showed that digestion is a chemical process driven by an acid resembling hydrochloric acid. His 1833 book listed 51 conclusions. St. Martin died in 1880 at 78, 27 years after Beaumont; his family let the body decompose and buried it deep to stop doctors taking the stomach.
Would you have let a doctor study you like this?
first_comment: Food on a string, pulled out hours later. What is the strangest experiment in medical history you know?
